items.role: Full relative-boundary finite PL T2×I rigidity from a proper pi1-isomorphism, GIVEN irreducibility, finite preimage compression, explicit helical target annulus, abelian cut and solid-torus extension.
items.after_birth_changes: Adopted canonical dependency phases; replaced broader closed-surface classification citations by an explicit finite rooted dual-tree collapse and disk-or-annulus neighborhood calculation.
proof_step_excerpts: 1.1 Choose a value $c$ of the $\lambda$ circle coordinate avoiding the finitely many vertex images of a common triangulation of that coordinate composed with $f$. Its preimage $F$ is a finite properly embedded cooriented PL surface. Indeed, on each source simplex it is a convex affine slice. Near a point in the smallest mixed source face, translation along a direction in that face with nonzero coordinate slope gives the same height change on every incident coface; it therefore gives the local product chart. Boundary faces give the corresponding half-space chart. This proves the PL surface and properness assertions without a transversality theorem. Its boundary consists of exactly one circle $C_i$ on each boundary torus, since the boundary map is a homeomorphism. Each maps once to the $\mu$ circle. Under $f_*$, every component's group image lies in the cyclic subgroup generated by $\mu$. Compress $F$ by [F1]. Each resulting component with boundary is injective in the same cyclic subgroup. Here is the required finite boundary-surface calculation. Root the triangle dual graph at an added outside vertex joined across all boundary edges, choose a finite spanning tree, and remove triangles in parent-before-child order, collapsing each across its now free parent edge. The remaining complex is a finite connected graph. Reading reduced edge words after collapsing a graph spanning tree gives its free fundamental group. A free group embedded in a cyclic group has rank at most one, since the commutator of two distinct generators is a nonempty reduced word. A regular disk-and-strip neighborhood of the remaining graph has the same finite PL surface type: reversing each triangle collapse adds a boundary flap along two consecutive edges, absorbed by the polygonal disk extension of [F4]. A tree neighborhood is a disk, by successively deleting leaf strips and disks. A rank-one graph consists of one circle with trees attached; deleting these leaf pieces leaves an orientable circle band, an annulus. Thus each injective boundary component surface is a supplied PL disk or annulus. A disk is impossible because either $C_i$ represents the nonzero $\mu$ element in $\pi_1(W)$. There is consequently one annulus $A$ joining $C_0$ to $C_1$. Discard the closed surface components; $A$ remains fundamental-group-injective. [given, F1, F4, construct]

2.1 Cut $W$ along $A$, obtaining $N$. The cut is connected: every cut component must meet one of the two copies of $A$, and the annulus obtained by cutting either boundary torus along its essential $C_i$ joins those copies. Each cut boundary torus is parametrized by the given boundary map. The boundary of $N$ is a single torus made from these two annuli and the two copies of $A$. Its finite standard parameter will also be supplied explicitly below. The annulus is two-sided and has a bicollar by the finite local-link and collar construction in [F1]. Apply [F2] to it. Since $\pi_1(W)\cong\mathbb Z^2$, we obtain $\pi_1(N)\cong\mathbb Z$, generated by the annulus circle, with injective map to $\pi_1(W)$. Irreducibility passes to $N$: a sphere in its interior bounds a ball in $W$ by hypothesis; the connected annulus $A$, disjoint from the sphere and reaching $\partial W$, cannot enter that ball, so the ball lies on the cut side and is contained in $N$. [given, F1, F2, step 1.1, construct]

2.2 We match the annulus map, including its possible winding in the other circle direction. Parametrize $A$ as $S^1\times[0,1]$, respecting the boundary labels. The $\lambda$ coordinate of $f|_A$ is constant $c$ on its boundary and has trivial induced group map, so [F5] lifts it to a real coordinate with boundary values $c$ and $c+m$ for some integer $m$. Let $$A_m=\{(u,c+ms,s):u\in S^1,\ 0\le s\le1\}\subset V.$$ Its boundary circles are the prescribed target circles. The boundary $\mu$ maps on the two ends of $A$ have the same degree, either one or minus one, since their loops are homotopic through $A$ and $f_*$ is injective. They extend to a PL annulus homeomorphism to $A_m$: subdivide both boundary circle maps compatibly in their cyclic order and match the intervening rectangular cells by the finite polygonal disk extensions of [F4]. If necessary compose with an integer twist in the $\mu$ coordinate, fixed on both boundary circles, to match the relative winding of $f_\mu|_A$. In detail the ratio of this chosen $\mu$ map and $f_\mu$ has a real lift by [F5], constant integers on the two boundary circles; one twist changes their difference by any prescribed integer. Choose that integer so both constants agree, and subtract it from the lift. Interpolation of the real lifts, of the interval coordinate, and of the two circle coordinates now gives a homotopy $f|_A\simeq a$ relative to its boundary, where $a:A\to A_m$ is the chosen PL homeomorphism. For the interval coordinate use its annulus parameter; for the $\lambda$ lift interpolate to $c+ms$. All boundary values are fixed. [F4, F5, step 1.1, construct]

3.1 Cut $V$ along $A_m$, obtaining a standard solid torus $V'$. Explicitly the PL shear $(u,v,s)\mapsto(u,v-ms,s)$, which is the identity on both boundary tori, takes $A_m$ to the constant-$\lambda$ annulus; its cut is $S^1\times[0,1]^2$. On $\partial N$ prescribe the original boundary maps on its two outside annuli and $a$ on both copies of $A$. They agree at the seams and give a PL homeomorphism $b:\partial N\to\partial V'$, supplying the promised torus parameter. Let $C=b^{-1}(\partial D^2\times\{s_0\})$ for a standard meridian of this cut solid torus. Its image is nullhomotopic in $V'$, hence in $V$. The map of this boundary loop under $f$ is homotopic in $V$ to its map under $b$: on the annulus copies use the relative homotopy of step 2.2 and elsewhere keep the original boundary map fixed. Since $\pi_1(N)\to\pi_1(W)\xrightarrow{f_*}\pi_1(V)$ is injective by step 2.1, $C$ is nullhomotopic in $N$. Apply [F3] to extend $b$ over a PL homeomorphism $N\to V'$. Its maps on the two annulus copies agree with their regluing identifications, so it descends to a PL homeomorphism $g:W\to V$ equal to $f$ on the boundary and to $a$ on $A$. [F3, F4, step 2.1, step 2.2, construct]

4.1 The maps $f,g$ induce the same map on fundamental groups, because they agree on a boundary torus whose inclusion induces an isomorphism on $\pi_1$: its composite with $f_*$ is the boundary inclusion isomorphism in $V$. Each circle-coordinate ratio $f_jg_j^{-1}$ therefore has a real lift by [F5], chosen zero on the first boundary torus. It is also zero on the second. To verify this, take a path in $A$ joining the two boundaries; step 2.2 gives a relative-boundary homotopy of the ratio on $A$ to the constant map, so its lift has zero endpoint difference on that path. The constant value on the second connected boundary is thus zero. Interpolate these real lifts in the two circle coordinates from $g$ to $f$, and linearly interpolate their interval coordinates. This gives a homotopy fixed on both boundary tori. At an interior point both interval coordinates lie strictly between zero and one, so every interpolated point does too; hence it is boundary-proper at every time. The lifts and twists involve finitely many coordinates and integers. The finite compression sequence, canonical transversal choices of [F2], cell maps and gluings introduce no choice principle. [given, F5, step 2.2, step 3.1, construct] ∎
